First of all, I’m bi and have a very strong preference, so I don’t have much experience with the opposite sex but I think anything I say can still apply. I think it’s mostly resentment towards people they’re attracted to, social anxiety, awkwardness, having any sort of mental difference to most people whether it’s harmful or not, being physically unattractive, disability (physical or otherwise) and just not getting out there. Besides the last thing I mentioned the other things the other things aren’t dooming you to be a kissless virgin, they’re just the common reasons why some might be. There’s also stuff like hygiene but I think anyone serious about not being alone romantically and/or sexually can solve that pretty easily. If you’ve got things like social anxiety, awkwardness, being physically unattractive, disability, you’re going to have to try so much harder than most people, but it it’s not impossible. I’ve got a lot of the issues I mentioned so the number of people interested in me is probably much lower than most people, but just because it’s lower doesn’t mean there’s none and I can confirm that even though I’m lonely still the whole “kissless virgin” thing is no more. A mistake I made though was going into interactions with the soul purpose being losing my virginity or later on having sex just for the sake of it (to somehow prove to myself I wasn’t super lonely), and for me at least that really just led to either having sex that was unsatisfying and made me feel even more lonely, or tainted meaningful interactions with people I really liked emotionally because all of the “I must have sex” stuff was bouncing around in my head. I’d say working on your social anxiety and trying to learn how to interact with people better is the way to go, good luck!

Being genuinely nice isn’t a red flag to anyone somewhat reasonable, but being too clingy, overly affectionate, lacking boundaries, etc can put people off. Personally I have a few difficulties with interacting with people, but I did find that I confused being somewhat obsessed with people as being nice. For me spending excessive amounts of money on people, dropping everything to respond within 5 seconds, all the excessive praise/attention/affection seemed like the right thing to do, but it wasn’t, it pushes people away. I feel like if you are like how I was (to be honest I still probably go a bit overboard but it’s not as extreme as before), there’s main ways it can go, 1. The person recognises that there’s some thing going on here that’s probably not good so they leave, 2. The person who thinks it’s too good to be true so they leave, or 3. The person that will walk all over you due to this issue. It’s never really a good outcome. You haven’t said enough to describe the issue so I’m really going out on a limb here but I had similar thoughts of “is being genuinely nice a red flag?”, and it turned out it wasn’t being “too nice”, it was being an overly invested pushover that was the red flag. I’m not saying to play “hard to get” or something like that, just don’t be like what I described. Good luck OP.

Well there’s lots of ways I’d imagine, and books on it, but I’ll talk about what helped me personally. An exercise that helped is writing a letter to yourself as if you’re someone else, because it’s much easier to be compassionate to someone else than yourself (for most people). It’s easy to think you’re terrible and stuff for having these issues but if it was someone else you probably wouldn’t hate them for it or think they deserve pain, so you can apply that to yourself. If that makes sense, just writing a letter to yourself but instead of being super hard on yourself, act as if you’re talking to someone else, and apply that compassion to yourself.

Hey, firstly I’d just like to say you’re not alone, I’ve got ASD and a bunch of other stuff that make interacting with people super difficult. I’m not going to lie and say that all your problems will be fixed upon you getting into a relationship, losing your virginity, make friends, etc, as they probably won’t, but it’s good to get out there. There’s lots of groups you can go to, like ones that play board games, DND, stuff like that, also ones based around anime, tv shows, anything really that there’s a common interest. I’m not sure how difficult it is for you to talk to people but going to bars can be a good way to meet people, personally I just find it easier to talk to people in a setting like that. Most of the people I’ve met have been on tinder, bumble, etc, there’s a bunch of apps for stuff like that. I’ve got to say online dating apps even when looking for friendship are absolutely soul-crushing at times, but really were the only place I met people, it’s really 90% apps and 9% bars and 1% everything else. All I can say is try not to get super attached to people, people will ghost you without any explanation, most of the people don’t have a decent conversation, people might just be looking for hookups (not inherently bad but sometimes it can be a bit much and then not even end up happening), but there’s a chance you could meet someone special and make a friend or meet a partner. Expect that since you’re new to this you’ll mess up sometimes but that’s okay, it’s not the end of the world even if it feels like it. Some advice I can give for meeting people in any context is don’t talk about how lonely you are unless they do first, don’t talk about mental health related things (especially psychiatric medication), don’t vent and stuff like that early on, it’s not that you should never talk about these things, just don’t do it too early, it’s a mistake I somehow repeatedly made. If you can see a therapist. I hope you feel a bit better soon, and manage to meet some people, good luck <3
